title: The Idiot
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
description: Dostoevsky's second great Petersburg novel, mapped from the terminus of the Warsaw railway through the salons and the merchant streets to the leafy summer resort of Pavlovsk, thirty kilometres south, where much of the second half unfolds. A companion to Crime and Punishment: the same city, a different fever.

route.summary: Prince Myshkin comes back to Russia from a Swiss sanatorium with nothing but a bundle, and shares a third-class carriage with the merchant Rogozhin. In the damp Petersburg fog the two men who will destroy each other over one woman meet by chance, and the whole tragedy is set in motion before the train even stops.
route.note: The novel opens on "the Warsaw and Petersburg railway" approaching the city; Dostoevsky does not name the terminus, but the Petersburg end of that line was the Warsaw Station (Varshavsky vokzal) on the Obvodny Canal, where the pin sits.

route.displayName: The Epanchin house, near the Litaynaya
route.summary: Myshkin arrives unannounced at his rich distant relations, the Epanchins, and is taken in half as a curiosity and half as a poor cousin. Here he meets Aglaya, the youngest daughter, and steps into the drawing-room world of the Petersburg gentry that will pull him one way while Nastasya Filippovna pulls him the other.
route.note: Dostoevsky places the general's house "near the Litaynaya" (Liteyny Prospekt) but invents the building; the pin marks a point on that fashionable avenue.

route.displayName: Nastasya Filippovna's flat, by the Great Theatre
route.summary: At her name-day party Nastasya Filippovna hurls Rogozhin's hundred thousand roubles into the fire and dares Ganya to snatch them out with his bare hands. It is the novel's most famous scene: the whole company's greed laid bare, and Nastasya choosing self-destruction over any of the men bidding for her.
route.note: Her flat is said to be "near the Great Theatre, just in the square there"—the Bolshoi Kamenny Theatre on what is now Theatre Square. The building is fictional; the pin marks the square.

route.summary: Myshkin walks down the Gorohovaya to the dark green merchant house where Rogozhin lives with his mother, past the money-changer's shop and up the dull red staircase. It is the brooding heart of the book: here Rogozhin shows him the knife and the Holbein Christ, and here, at the very end, the two men will keep watch over Nastasya's body.
route.note: The Gorohovaya (Gorokhovaya Street) and its crossing with the Sadovaya are named exactly; the merchant house itself is Dostoevsky's invention, pinned to that intersection.

route.summary: The summer half of the novel moves out to Pavlovsk, the fashionable resort south of the city, where the gentry gather to hear the orchestra at the Vauxhall pavilion. Into that decorous evening crowd Nastasya Filippovna walks with her drunken retinue and calls out a scandal, breaking Petersburg society open in front of the Epanchins.
route.note: Pavlovsk and its Vauxhall are named in the text. The pin marks the Pavlovsk Vokzal, the concert pavilion beside the railway in the park; the original building no longer stands.

route.summary: Nastasya flees her own wedding to Myshkin and runs to Rogozhin, who kills her that night with the knife. Myshkin comes to the dark house and the two men lie down together beside her covered body until dawn. The novel ends where it began, on the Gorohovaya, with the prince's mind finally gone.
route.note: The final scene returns to Rogozhin's house on the Gorohovaya, the same invented merchant house pinned to the Gorokhovaya and Sadovaya crossing.
